documents: He et al. 2022, Groundwater 60(3): 434-450, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: studies on the subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater for mountain glaciers are relatively limited

steps.action: The authors review published rates of subglacial meltwater recharge and infiltration, mostly assigned or simulated for ice sheets (0 to 36 mm/year).
steps.quote: Previous studies attempted to quantify the rate of subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater in different areas.

steps.action: The authors pose the aim: quantify subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater under the Dongkemadi Glacier with HGS and evaluate the controlling factors under future climate.
steps.quote: [...] aim of this paper is to use the HydroGesSphere (HGS) model (Aquanty 2015) to quantify the amount of subglacial meltwater recharge

steps.action: The authors take climate series for 1971-2020 reconstructed from four surrounding meteorological stations (Gao et al. 2012) and report temperature and PDD trends (Figure 2).
steps.quote: previous studies have reconstructed the climate data from four meteorological stations

steps.action: The authors take glacier thickness from the Farinotti et al. (2019) consensus ice-thickness estimate, which Gao et al. (2021) correlated with more than 7000 GPR points.
steps.quote: Thicknesses of the Dongkemadi Glacier used in the model were obtained from the global glacier thickness distribution data by Farinotti et al. (2019)

steps.action: The authors parameterize the decrease of permeability and specific storage with depth using their own earlier depth relations (Kuang and Jiao 2014; Kuang et al. 2021), with two lithologies taken from a 1:500,000 map.
steps.quote: the Kuang and Jiao (2014)’s model was used to describe the decrease of permeability with depth

steps.action: The authors build a 3D HGS model (9068 triangular elements, 20 layers, 10 km deep) with a glacier equivalent-head boundary (ice/water density ratio 0.92), a constant-head river and precipitation-infiltration flux.
steps.quote: The specified head boundary was used to calculate the rate of subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater.

steps.action: The authors set warming scenarios of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 °C (precipitation +10%/°C) and compute glacier mass balance with a degree-day factor model using cited DDF values.
steps.quote: The degree-day factor model was used to calculate the variation of the thickness of the Dongkemadi Glacier in the next 50 years.

steps.action: The authors fit linear relations of DDF with elevation for the Da and Xiao Dongkemadi glaciers (R2 = 0.15 and 0.52; Figure 10).
steps.quote: The DDF of the Da Dongkemadi Glacier increases with elevation by about

steps.action: The authors project glacier area and mean thickness to 2070 under each scenario (largest reductions 2.69% and 26.17%; Figure 12).
steps.quote: Both glacier area and average glacier thickness show decreasing trends and the trends become more and more significant.

steps.action: Because the projected area change is small, the authors fix the glacier boundary in the numerical model for the 50-year run.
steps.quote: it can be assumed that the glacier boundary will remain unchanged in the next 50 years in the numerical model

steps.action: The authors run a steady-state HGS model with the initial glacier thickness to obtain mean subglacial recharge of 4.58 mm/year (6.33% of total groundwater recharge); no calibration is reported.
steps.quote: The simulated rate of multi-year average subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater is 4.58 mm/year by the steady-state flow model

steps.action: The authors compare the simulated rate with rates assigned or simulated in earlier, mainly ice-sheet, studies and call it consistent.
In transient runs for 2021-2070, the authors vary K and P by 5, 10 and 15% and T by 0.5 to 1.5 °C, and report how the recharge rate and its share change (Figure 13).
steps.quote: When K increases by 5%, 10%, and 15%, the rate of annual mean subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater increases by 0.017, 0.034, and 0.051 mm/year

steps.action: The authors map the simulated hydraulic head along the A-A' profile and in the z = 5000 m plane under each factor change (Figures 14 and 15).
steps.quote: Hydraulic head increases with the increase of precipitation

steps.action: The authors note that permafrost is omitted, so the simulated recharge may overestimate the real value.
steps.quote: the simulated amount of subglacial meltwater recharging groundwater may be greater than the real value

steps.action: The authors add glacier loading efficiency (0.2, 0.6, 1.0) to the steady-state model; recharge falls by 0.36 to 1.81%, so loading is neglected.
steps.quote: when the loading efficiency is 0.2, 0.6, and 1.0, the multi-year average rate of subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater decreased

steps.action: The authors keep the estimate of 4.58 mm/year and the ranking of factor influence (K above T and P).
steps.quote: The annual mean subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater simulated by the HGS model is 4.58 mm/year

tree.answer: Subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater beneath a Tibetan mountain glacier; assumed, not established
No; subglacial meltwater is extremely difficult to measure
Quantify the recharge rate and the effects of K, P and T under future climate
Conditions set as model scenarios (warming 0.5-1.5 °C, K and P +5-15%)
Sensitivity runs and a loading-efficiency test; no comparison with observed heads or flows
Estimate of 4.58 mm/year kept, with ranking K > T > P
Reviewers thanked; no review file supplied

end.claim: The HGS model gives a mean subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater of 4.58 mm/year (6.33% of total recharge) in the Dongkemadi River Basin; hydraulic conductivity influences it more than temperature or precipitation.

decisive_move.sentence: The steady-state HGS run with the equivalent-head boundary built from the Farinotti et al. (2019) thickness produces the 4.58 mm/year figure; without it there is no estimate.

gates.evidence: No new data were acquired; all inputs are cited data products. The estimate was not calibrated or tested against observed heads, discharge or recharge. Its only comparison is with a broad range of mostly ice-sheet values (0 to 36 mm/year), which it could hardly fail. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: two-dimensional Saint Venant equation for surface flow
conversion of permeability to hydraulic conductivity, K = kρg/μ

novelty_claims.quote: This is the first comprehensive study on subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater in the Tibetan Plateau.
This study makes the first attempt to build a numerical groundwater flow model takes into account the Dongkemadi Glacier

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: the glacier area and thickness projections to 2070 (-2.7% and -26.2% at +1.5 °C) are scenario projections that were not scored, status none; the ranking of factor influence (K > T > P) holds only within the chosen perturbations, a regularity_in_range. The ranking depends on the perturbation sizes the authors chose (inference). No uncertainty interval is given for 4.58 mm/year; the resolution is only the spread of the sensitivity runs. The paper reports no calibration or validation of the groundwater model against observed heads, river discharge or tracer data (inference from absence). The comparison with previous studies rests on ice-sheet values from different settings. The text refers to Equation 7 and Figure 11 where Equations 5-7 and Figure 10 seem intended, and the abstract gives 4.58 mm without '/year'. Reviewers are thanked, but no review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a model-based scenario estimate with no rivals, no repeated natural cases and no new capability, and fits none of the listed compositions. Triangulation is absent: the checks performed here are robustness runs and one literature comparison.

disagreements.target: Lemieux et al. (2008b), ice-sheet loading effects on subglacial recharge
disagreements.support: A loading-efficiency test shows recharge falls by at most 1.81%, so loading that matters under a 4.5 km ice sheet is negligible under a 96.5 m mountain glacier.
disagreements.quote: The impact of the weight of the Dongkemadi Glacier on subglacial meltwater recharge to groundwater should be very small and can be neglected.

alternatives_considered.reason: widely used in subglacial groundwater modeling; avoids characterizing the recharge rate directly

alternatives_considered.chosen: ice/water density ratio of 0.92 for the equivalent head
alternatives_considered.alternatives: proportions of glacier thickness from 70% to 92% used in other studies

alternatives_considered.chosen: degree-day factor model for glacier mass balance
alternatives_considered.alternatives: energy balance model; field measurement; geodetic survey
alternatives_considered.reason: widely used and refined; few glaciers have long-term observations

alternatives_considered.alternatives: HGS freeze-thaw modules; permafrost as a low-K barrier
alternatives_considered.reason: permafrost distribution and thickness are very difficult to determine

alternatives_considered.alternatives: including flow in the unsaturated zone
alternatives_considered.reason: similar to existing subglacial recharge models
